stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the blue swatch?
stimulus: Synthetic dyes were first produced in 1856, so textile historians can often date a fabric by testing its colorants. A newly catalogued set of 214 swatches from an English mill mostly meets expectations: nearly all contain synthetic dyes, which fits the mill's records of weaving them in the 1870s. One blue swatch, however, contains only natural indigo. The mill's ledgers show that it had switched to synthetic blue by 1868, so researchers suspect the swatch was cut from older stock rather than woven alongside the rest.
choices: It contains synthetic colorants, as do nearly all of the swatches in the set.
It was likely made earlier than most of the set, though it was kept with 1870s cloth.
It shows that the mill never used synthetic dyes when producing its blue cloth.
It was woven in the 1870s with natural indigo the mill purchased after 1868.
explanation: Put together every sentence about the blue swatch. It contains only natural indigo, the mill had switched to synthetic blue by 1868, and researchers suspect it came from older stock. Together these mean it was probably made before the rest of the set, even though it was stored with cloth from the 1870s. Choice B states that consequence and stops there.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Nearly all the swatches contain synthetic dyes, but the passage singles out the blue one because it contains only natural indigo.

C.why: You stretched one swatch into a claim about everything the mill made. The ledgers actually show the mill was using synthetic blue by 1868, so the text points the other way.

D.why: You mixed up the dates. Researchers think the swatch was not woven in the 1870s with the rest, and nothing says the mill bought natural indigo after 1868, the year by which it had switched to synthetic blue.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the Corran Bridge?
stimulus: Most suspension bridges built in the Calder region during the 1930s used shallow stiffening girders, a choice that kept them light and inexpensive. The Corran Bridge was an exception. Its engineers insisted on a deep open truss, which raised the bridge's weight and cost by nearly a fifth. However, when a severe windstorm struck in 1950, several neighboring spans twisted so badly that they had to be closed, while the Corran Bridge needed only minor repairs.
choices: It used a shallow girder like nearby spans, but it was repaired more quickly.
It became the model for every suspension bridge built in the region after 1950.
Its truss made it lighter than nearby spans, which reduced its twisting in wind.
Its deep truss increased its cost but also helped it come through a severe storm.
explanation: The text tells you two things about the Corran Bridge's deep truss. It added nearly a fifth to the cost, and after the 'However' pivot, the bridge needed only minor repairs when nearby spans failed. Choice D joins the drawback and the benefit of that one feature.

A.why: You gave the exception the group's feature. The other bridges used shallow girders. The Corran Bridge is set apart precisely because it used a deep truss.

B.why: This sounds like a natural next step, but the passage says nothing about later bridges copying the Corran design.

C.why: You got the weight backward. The truss made the bridge heavier, not lighter. The shallow girders were the light option.

stem: What does the text indicate about the Halvern district?
stimulus: The 1962 master plan for the city of Delmont separated residential, commercial, and industrial land into distinct zones, and nearly every district built under it followed that rule. The Halvern district did not. Because its land had been subdivided before the plan was adopted, planners allowed its existing ground-floor shops beneath apartments to remain. Recent travel surveys suggest that Halvern residents make fewer car trips for errands than residents of any other Delmont district.
choices: Its mixed uses predate the plan, and its residents seem to drive less for errands.
It kept housing and shops in separate zones, as the plan required of every district.
Its example led planners to abandon zoning separation throughout the rest of Delmont.
It was subdivided after 1962, so planners designed it with shops beneath apartments.
explanation: Collect the Halvern sentences. Its shops beneath apartments were already there before the 1962 plan, and surveys suggest its residents make fewer car trips for errands. Choice A combines both facts and keeps the hedge, since 'seem' matches 'suggest'.

B.why: You described the rule the rest of the city followed. Halvern is the district that did not separate housing from shops.

C.why: The passage never says Halvern changed how the rest of Delmont was zoned. This choice invents a consequence the text does not support.

D.why: You reversed the order of events. The land was subdivided before the plan, and planners allowed existing shops to remain rather than designing new ones.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the lung-resident memory B cells?
stimulus: Most memory B cells produced after a vaccination circulate in the blood for months and then gradually decline. In a study of mice immunized against an influenza strain, however, researchers found a small population of these cells that had settled in lung tissue itself. The lung-resident cells were far fewer than the circulating ones, but when the mice were later exposed to the virus, they began producing antibodies days sooner. The researchers concluded that location, rather than number, may matter most for early protection.
choices: They circulated in the blood for months and then declined, as most memory cells do.
They gave the immunized mice complete protection against every strain of influenza.
Though fewer than the circulating cells, they began making antibodies days sooner.
They outnumbered the circulating cells, which explains their faster antibody response.
explanation: The text describes the lung-resident cells in two ways. They were 'far fewer' than the circulating cells, and they produced antibodies 'days sooner.' Choice C combines that contrast: small in number, but faster.

A.why: You described the typical memory cell, not the exception. The passage sets the lung-resident cells apart from cells that circulate and decline.

B.why: The study tested one influenza strain and measured how quickly antibodies appeared. It never claims complete protection, let alone protection against every strain.

D.why: You confused speed with number. The cells were faster but far fewer, which is exactly why the researchers credited location rather than number.

stem: What does the text indicate about the chart attributed to the Genoese workshop?
stimulus: Sixteenth-century portolan charts generally recorded coastlines in remarkable detail while leaving the interiors of continents blank. A chart attributed to a Genoese workshop is unusual in this respect: it fills the interior of North Africa with rivers and towns. Comparison with travelers' accounts, however, shows that many of those inland features are misplaced by hundreds of kilometers, even though the chart's coastline is as accurate as that of any contemporary chart.
choices: Like other charts of its time, it leaves the interior of North Africa blank.
Unlike most charts of its time, it depicts the interior, though often inaccurately.
Its coastline is badly misplaced, while its interior rivers and towns are accurate.
It was the chart most widely consulted by Mediterranean navigators of its era.
explanation: Two sentences describe this chart. It is unusual because it fills in the interior, and many of those inland features are misplaced. Choice B combines its difference from other charts with the problem in what it adds.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Most charts left the interior blank. This one is notable because it does not.

C.why: You swapped the two features. The coastline is accurate and the interior features are misplaced, not the other way around.

D.why: This sounds like a scholarly fact, but the passage never says anything about how widely the chart was used.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Kesselopteris arcana?
stimulus: Most plant fossils recovered from the Kessel shale belong to genera that still have living relatives, which lets researchers estimate the ancient climate from where those relatives grow today. A fern identified in the shale in 2021, Kesselopteris arcana, cannot be used this way. Its leaves combine structural features of two separate fern families, a combination found in no living fern, and the species is known only from fossils preserved in the shale.
choices: It appears to be extinct, so it offers no modern range for inferring climate.
It belongs to a genus whose living relatives reveal the shale's ancient climate.
It is the most frequently studied fossil fern recovered from the Kessel shale.
It belongs to one of two living fern families, though its leaves are unusual.
explanation: Combine the facts. The fern is known only from fossils, and no living fern shares its leaf structure, so it appears to be extinct. That is why it 'cannot be used this way': it has no living relatives whose range could point to a climate. Choice A states this small logical consequence.

B.why: You described the rest of the fossils, not the exception. The passage introduces this fern as the one that cannot be used to estimate climate.

C.why: 'Frequently studied' sounds scientific, but nothing in the text says how often the fern has been studied. It was only identified in 2021.

D.why: You misread the category. The fern combines features of two families, a combination no living fern has. The text never places it in either family.

stem: What does the text indicate about Dunmore Spring?
stimulus: Springs fed by shallow aquifers typically shrink within weeks of a drought's onset, because the water they release fell as rain only recently. Dunmore Spring, in an otherwise drought-sensitive valley, kept flowing steadily through a fourteen-month dry spell. Isotope analysis indicates that its water entered the ground roughly 3,000 years ago, suggesting that the spring draws on a deep aquifer rather than on the shallow ones that feed its neighbors.
choices: Like nearby springs, it is fed by recent rainfall held in a shallow aquifer.
Its flow will remain unaffected by any future drought, however long it lasts.
Its water fell as rain recently, which let it recover quickly after the drought.
Its water likely comes from a deep source, which helps explain its steady flow.
explanation: Gather the sentences about Dunmore Spring. It kept flowing through a long drought, and its water is about 3,000 years old, 'suggesting' a deep aquifer. Choice D links the deep source to the steady flow and keeps the hedge with 'likely'.

A.why: You described the neighboring springs. The text sets Dunmore apart from springs fed by recent rain in shallow aquifers.

B.why: The spring survived one fourteen-month dry spell. The text gives no basis for predicting it will survive every future drought.

C.why: You got the water's age wrong. It entered the ground about 3,000 years ago, and the spring never stopped flowing, so there was nothing to recover from.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes the warbler population that nests in the geothermal valley?
stimulus: Nearly all populations of the gray-crowned warbler leave their northern breeding grounds each autumn and spend the winter in Central America. Banding records show that one population, nesting along a geothermal river valley in the Rockies, is an exception: its members remain through the winter, feeding on insects that stay active near the warm water. That same dependence, however, leaves the population vulnerable. In years when the valley's hot springs weaken, its numbers drop sharply.
choices: It spends winter in Central America, as the species' other populations do.
It migrates north each autumn to feed on insects near the valley's hot springs.
The warm water that lets it stay through winter also leaves it open to decline.
It is growing faster than other populations because it avoids risky migration.
explanation: The passage names one factor, the valley's warm water, and gives it two effects. It lets the birds stay through winter by keeping insects active, and it exposes them to sharp declines when the springs weaken. Choice C is the only one that combines both.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Other populations winter in Central America. This one stays put.

B.why: You treated a question of whether the birds migrate as a question of which direction they go. This population does not migrate at all. It remains in the valley through the winter.

D.why: The text never compares growth rates, and it actually stresses that this population is vulnerable. The claim about faster growth is invented.

stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Lecidea ardens?
stimulus: Most lichens on the granite outcrops of the Sierra Ventosa grow only on north-facing rock, where shade slows evaporation. Ecologist Paula Ireton found one exception, a crust lichen she named Lecidea ardens, spreading across the sunniest south faces. However, it appears there only where seabirds roost: their droppings supply nitrogen that lets the lichen build pigments shielding it from intense light. Away from roosts, Ireton recorded no L. ardens on south faces at all.
choices: It is limited to shaded north-facing rock, where slow evaporation keeps it moist.
It grows on sunny rock but only where seabird droppings supply needed nitrogen.
It crowds out other lichens on south-facing rock wherever seabirds happen to roost.
It survives strong sunlight by drawing extra water from the droppings of seabirds.
explanation: Collect every sentence about L. ardens. It is the exception that grows on the sunniest south faces. It appears there only where seabirds roost, because their droppings supply nitrogen for its light-shielding pigments. Away from roosts there is none. Put those together and you get choice B: sunny rock, but only with nitrogen from seabird droppings.

A.why: You described the group, not the exception. Shaded north-facing rock is where most lichens grow. The text sets L. ardens apart because it grows on the sunniest south faces.

C.why: You added a claim that sounds scientific but isn't in the text. The passage never compares L. ardens with other lichens on south faces, so you can't point to a line that says it crowds them out.

D.why: You got the right source and the wrong benefit. The droppings supply nitrogen, which the lichen uses to build protective pigments. Water is never mentioned. Read the choice to the end: the first half sounds right and the second half is wrong.

stem: What does the text indicate about the firms in Callis?
stimulus: When the province of Merrow raised its minimum wage in 2019, most of the 40 distribution firms studied by economist Dana Okafor cut overnight shifts. Firms in the town of Callis did the opposite, adding shifts. Okafor attributes this to Callis's isolation: as the only large employers for miles, those firms had long paid below what workers would earn elsewhere and had struggled to fill night positions. The higher mandated wage, she suggests, likely drew enough applicants to staff those vacant shifts.
choices: They cut overnight shifts once the higher provincial minimum wage took effect.
The higher wage likely helped them staff night shifts they had been unable to fill.
They raised pay above the new minimum to compete with employers in nearby towns.
Their experience shows that higher minimum wages increase hiring in most regions.
explanation: Gather what the text says about Callis. Its firms added shifts. They had paid low wages and struggled to fill night positions. Okafor suggests the higher mandated wage likely drew enough applicants to staff those vacancies. Choice B combines these facts and keeps the hedge: the higher wage 'likely' helped them fill shifts that had been sitting empty.

A.why: You described the group instead of the exception. Most of the firms cut overnight shifts. The text says the Callis firms 'did the opposite, adding shifts.'

C.why: You missed the reason Okafor gives. The Callis firms were 'the only large employers for miles,' so there were no nearby employers to compete with. The text also never says they paid more than the new minimum.

D.why: You stretched one town into a general rule. Most firms in the study cut shifts, and Okafor ties the Callis result to its unusual isolation. Nothing in the text supports a claim about most regions.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Legume cover crops such as clover and vetch are usually planted in autumn and add nitrogen to the soil only after farmers till them under in spring. Agronomist Lena Okafor's field trials with a cowpea line called Ridgeback, however, point to a different path. Ridgeback is sown in late summer, fixes nitrogen through the fall, and is killed by the first hard frost. Its residue then breaks down on the surface over winter, releasing nitrogen for a spring crop without any tilling at all.
choices: Unlike many legume cover crops, Ridgeback can supply nitrogen to a later crop without being tilled into the soil.
Legume cover crops such as clover and vetch must be tilled under in spring before they release any nitrogen.
Ridgeback survives winter frost, so it can keep fixing nitrogen until farmers till it under in the spring.
Ridgeback fixes more nitrogen than clover or vetch, so farmers are replacing those crops with the new cowpea.
explanation: Collect every sentence about Ridgeback: it is sown in late summer, a frost kills it, and its residue releases nitrogen 'without any tilling at all.' Now set that against the group in the first sentence, whose members release nitrogen only after they are tilled under. Put together, those sentences say Ridgeback feeds a later crop without tilling, and the whole passage is built to show that. Choice A says exactly that and nothing more.

B.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The first sentence does say this about clover and vetch, but it only sets up the contrast. The passage is about Ridgeback, so this choice is too narrow to be the main idea.

C.why: You got Ridgeback's key fact backwards. The text says the first hard frost kills Ridgeback and that it needs no tilling. This choice has it surviving the frost and being tilled, which is how the group behaves, not Ridgeback.

D.why: The passage never compares how much nitrogen each crop fixes, and it never says farmers are switching. This sounds like a reasonable scientific claim, but you can't point to any line that supports it.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Static stretching just before exercise has repeatedly been found to reduce jump height. Kinesiologist Mara Lindqvist suspected that the effect depends on habit. In her study, competitive gymnasts, who hold long stretches every day, jumped no lower after stretching, while recreational runners of similar fitness jumped about 4 percent lower. Lindqvist concludes that years of stretching may allow the body to adapt, though she cautions that her sample included only 40 athletes.
choices: Lindqvist's results suggest that athletes who stretch daily may not lose jumping power after static stretching.
Static stretching before exercise lowers jump height in athletes regardless of how often they usually stretch.
Recreational runners in Lindqvist's study jumped about 4 percent lower after holding static stretches.
Lindqvist's study shows that daily stretching raises the jump height of trained athletes in every sport.
explanation: The general finding comes first, and then the passage turns to the gymnasts, who are the exception: they 'jumped no lower after stretching.' Lindqvist explains the difference by habit, and she hedges twice, with 'may allow' and the small sample. Choice A combines the exception with its explanation and keeps the hedge ('suggest,' 'may'). That covers the whole passage without claiming more than it does.

B.why: You described the group and missed the exception. The first sentence states the general pattern, but the gymnasts did not jump lower, so the text directly rules out 'regardless of how often they usually stretch.'

C.why: This is accurate, but it covers only one sentence. You can find the line that proves it, but the passage does much more than this, which makes it too narrow to be the main idea.

D.why: The gymnasts' jumps did not drop. Nothing says they went up, and nothing extends the finding to 'every sport.' The choice also drops Lindqvist's caution about her 40-athlete sample.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Astronomers have found six planets orbiting a nearby star they have nicknamed Arden. Planets that form together from a disk of gas around a young star are expected to circle it in the direction it spins, and the five inner planets do. The outermost planet, however, travels in the opposite direction, though its path is just as nearly circular as the others'. For this reason, the research team argues that the planet most likely formed elsewhere and was later captured by Arden's gravity.
choices: Arden's outermost planet differs from its neighbors in the direction of its orbit, suggesting it formed elsewhere.
Arden's outermost planet differs from its neighbors in the shape of its orbit, suggesting it formed elsewhere.
The five inner planets orbit Arden in the direction it spins, as planets formed in a shared disk usually do.
Arden's outermost planet is the first ever found to orbit backward, which proves that it was later captured.
explanation: Gather what the text says about the outermost planet. It orbits opposite to the star's spin, and its path is 'just as nearly circular' as the others', so direction is the only thing that sets it apart. From that difference the team infers that it 'most likely formed elsewhere.' Choice A names the right difference and keeps the team's hedged conclusion.

B.why: You mixed up the category the planet is an exception in. The text says its orbit is as circular as its neighbors'. It differs in direction, not shape. The first half of this choice reads correctly, so check the second half before you pick it.

C.why: You described the group instead of the exception. The five inner planets are the background the outer planet is compared against. This statement is true, but it leaves out the planet the passage is actually about.

D.why: The text never says this is the first such planet, and the team says only that capture is 'most likely.' Changing that to 'proves' claims far more than the passage supports.

stem: Based on the text, which choice does NOT accurately describe Mandarin Chinese?
stimulus: Most of the world's languages mark grammatical tense, signaling on the verb whether an event is past, present, or future. Mandarin Chinese, however, generally does not. Instead, its speakers use aspect markers, short words that show whether an action is finished or still ongoing, and leave the timing of an event to context. Linguist Wen Liu argues that this does not make Mandarin less precise; it simply moves the work of placing events in time from the verb to the surrounding conversation.
choices: It uses short words to show whether an action has been completed.
It usually marks on the verb whether an event is past or future.
It relies on context to convey when an event takes place.
It is not made less precise by the way it handles time.
explanation: Marking past, present, or future on the verb is what the text says *most* languages do. It then says Mandarin, 'however, generally does not.' So B describes the group, not the exception, and it is the one statement the text contradicts. Each of the other three matches a sentence about Mandarin that you can point to.

A.why: You mixed up aspect and tense. Showing whether an action is finished is aspect, and the text says that is exactly what Mandarin's aspect markers do. This is the category confusion the passage is built around, and it made a true statement look false.

C.why: You suspected that 'relies on context' says more than the passage does. But the text states that speakers 'leave the timing of an event to context,' so the choice simply restates the text.

D.why: You treated this as an unsupported judgment. The last sentence reports Liu's view that the system 'does not make Mandarin less precise,' so the statement is backed directly by the text.

stem: Based on the text, which choice does NOT accurately describe grocery retail in Okafor's study?
stimulus: After a regional minimum wage rose by 12 percent, economist Rita Okafor found that employment fell modestly in most of the low-wage sectors she studied. Grocery retail appeared to be the exception, since its number of workers held steady. However, Okafor also found that grocers cut their employees' average weekly hours by about 6 percent, so total hours worked in the sector dropped by roughly as much as elsewhere. The stability of grocery employment, she concludes, may have been more apparent than real.
choices: It avoided the drop in total labor seen in other low-wage sectors.
Its number of workers stayed level after the wage increase.
Its employees were given fewer hours per week on average.
Its total hours fell by about as much as in other sectors.
explanation: The sentence after 'However' says total hours worked in grocery retail fell 'by roughly as much as elsewhere.' So grocers did not avoid the drop in labor. They took it as shorter hours instead of fewer workers. A describes the appearance that Okafor's finding corrects, so A is the choice that does NOT fit.

B.why: You read Okafor's conclusion that the stability was 'more apparent than real' as a claim that headcount actually fell. It didn't. The text says the number of workers 'held steady.' What fell was the hours.

C.why: You may have thought this detail belonged to the other sectors. The 6 percent cut in average weekly hours is reported for grocers specifically, so the statement is true.

D.why: You treated this as a stretch beyond the data. To get there, though, you only combine the two facts about grocers, as the method asks: hours per worker fell, so total hours fell 'by roughly as much as elsewhere,' which the text states outright.

stem: Based on the text, which choice does NOT accurately describe the yellow-rumped warbler population Whitcombe studied?
stimulus: Of the warbler species that nest in the Appalachian forests surveyed by ornithologist Dana Whitcombe, all but one migrate south before October. The exception, a population of yellow-rumped warblers, stays through the winter by switching from insects to the waxy berries of bayberry shrubs, which most warblers cannot digest. Whitcombe notes that this diet ties the birds closely to bayberry stands: in winters when the berry crop failed, local counts of the population dropped sharply.
choices: It remains in the Appalachian forests through the winter months.
It eats a food that most other warblers are unable to digest.
It switches to eating berries after it migrates south in autumn.
Its winter numbers depend partly on the size of the berry crop.
explanation: This is a half-right choice. The birds do switch to berries, but the text says they make that switch so they can stay *instead of* migrating. Flying south before October is what the other warblers do. C attaches the group's behavior to the exception, so it does NOT describe this population.

A.why: You assigned the group's behavior to the exception and assumed this population migrates like the others. The text calls it the exception because it 'stays through the winter.'

B.why: You read 'which most warblers cannot digest' as describing the yellow-rumped warblers' own limits. The clause describes other warblers. This population eats the berries, so the statement is true.

D.why: You thought 'depend partly' went beyond the evidence. The final sentence links failed berry crops to sharp drops in local counts, so tying winter numbers to the crop is a small, supported inference.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Folklorist Ines Varga recorded 63 versions of the "Fox at the Ferry" tale in the inland farming villages of the Drava basin. In nearly all of them, the fox's trick fails and the ferryman drives it off. However, the nine versions Varga collected in the river-port town of Brodvar end with the fox keeping its prize, and tellers there call the fox clever rather than greedy. Varga suggests that Brodvar's trading families may have favored a hero who profits from a quick bargain, though she cautions that nine versions is a small sample.
choices: Versions of the tale told in one port town reward the fox where inland versions punish it, possibly reflecting the town's trading culture.
Varga recorded far more versions of the tale in the basin's inland villages than she recorded in the river-port town of Brodvar.
In most versions of the tale that Varga collected, tellers praise the fox as clever and allow it to keep the prize it wins.
Port towns throughout the Drava basin tell tales that reward tricksters, a pattern caused by their long history of river trade.
explanation: The passage sets up the usual inland ending (the fox fails), then uses "However" to bring in what it is really about: Brodvar's versions, where the fox wins. It closes with a hedged explanation ("may have favored"). Choice A covers both the gap between the two groups and the tentative reason, and it keeps the word "possibly" to match Varga's caution.

B.why: 63 is more than 9, so this is true. But it is a side detail about how many versions were collected. It says nothing about how the endings differ, which is what the passage is about. You picked a statement because you could check it, not because it covers the whole text.

C.why: You took a fact about the exception and applied it to the whole group. Only the nine Brodvar versions praise the fox. In nearly all of the 63 inland versions the fox fails and is driven off.

D.why: The passage discusses one port town, and Varga only suggests a reason while warning that her sample is small. This choice spreads the finding to every port town and calls a tentative explanation a proven cause.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Exercise physiologists asked 30 middle-distance runners to complete a 5-kilometer time trial at 32°C. Compared with their times in cool conditions, most runners finished about 6 percent slower. However, the eight runners who had spent the previous two weeks training in a heated chamber slowed by only about 2 percent, and their core temperatures rose more gradually during the trial. The researchers conclude that heat training likely reduces, but does not remove, the performance cost of running in hot weather.
choices: Runners who trained in heat beforehand slowed much less in hot conditions than the other runners did, though they still ran slower than in the cool.
Most of the runners in the study finished their 5-kilometer time trial at 32°C about 6 percent slower than they did in cool conditions.
Runners who trained in a heated chamber for two weeks ran as fast at 32°C as they did in cool conditions, with no loss in performance.
Training in a heated chamber improves runners' times in both hot and cool conditions, which makes it the best preparation for any race.
explanation: The pivot word "However" brings in the heat-trained group, and the last sentence sums up what the passage is about: heat training shrinks the slowdown (2 percent instead of 6) but doesn't eliminate it. Choice A states both the gap between the groups and the limit set by "does not remove."

B.why: This describes the main group, not the exception the passage builds toward. It's accurate, but it covers only one sentence and leaves out the comparison with the heat-trained runners.

C.why: You found the right group and then attached the wrong claim to it. The heat-trained runners still slowed by about 2 percent, and the researchers say heat training does not remove the cost. You lose this one if you stop reading once the opening words look right.

D.why: The study tested heat-trained runners only at 32°C. It says nothing about their times in cool conditions and never ranks heat training against other kinds of preparation.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
stimulus: Agronomists comparing a new sorghum line, DR-7, with a standard variety over six growing seasons found that DR-7's roots reached nearly twice as deep. In the three dry seasons, that depth let DR-7 draw on moisture the standard variety could not reach, and it outyielded the standard by about a quarter. In the one unusually wet season, however, DR-7's deep roots sat in waterlogged soil, and it yielded less than the standard. The same trait, the researchers conclude, was both DR-7's advantage and its weakness.
choices: DR-7's deeper roots gave it higher yields than the standard variety in dry seasons but lower yields than the standard in a very wet one.
In each of the three dry seasons in the trial, DR-7 outyielded the standard sorghum variety by about a quarter of the standard's yield.
DR-7 outyielded the standard variety in every season of the trial because its roots reached nearly twice as deep into the soil.
Farmers should replace standard sorghum with DR-7 in any region where dry growing seasons are more common than unusually wet ones.
explanation: The final sentence puts the middle details together: one trait, deep roots, helped DR-7 in dry seasons and hurt it in the wet one. Choice A gives the gap in both directions, ahead of the standard variety when it's dry and behind it when it's wet, and ties both to the roots.

B.why: This is true, but it covers only the dry seasons. It leaves out the wet season, where the same roots became a weakness, and that turn is the passage's point.

C.why: You read the dry-season result as the whole story. In the wet season DR-7 yielded less than the standard, so "every season" is wrong. The passage names the right cause (deep roots), but this choice gets the result wrong.

D.why: The passage reports trial results and never recommends anything to farmers. It also has data from only one wet season, which isn't enough to support a rule about where to plant DR-7.

subtype_name: Which choice best describes X / what does the text indicate about X
